body:
Introduction: The Beginning of Gandhian Mass Politics

The Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda movements marked an important stage in the development of India's national movement. Between 1917 and 1918, Mahatma Gandhi intervened in 3 local struggles involving indigo cultivators, industrial workers and peasants facing land revenue demands. Although their immediate objectives were different, all 3 demonstrated how ordinary people could organise against injustice through disciplined, nonviolent collective action.

These struggles brought Gandhi into close contact with rural and urban communities whose everyday economic difficulties had not always received sustained attention in national politics. They also established working relationships between Gandhi and local leaders who would later contribute to the freedom movement.

Gandhi's Return to India in 1915

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915. In South Africa, he had organised campaigns against racial discrimination and developed the method of protest known as satyagraha.

Gopal Krishna Gokhale, whom Gandhi regarded as his political mentor, advised him to understand conditions in India before undertaking major political action. Gandhi consequently travelled through different regions, observing the circumstances of ordinary people.

His early interventions arose from specific local grievances rather than from a single nationwide political programme. Peasants and workers sought his assistance because they faced problems involving cultivation, wages or government revenue demands.

Meaning and Principles of Satyagraha

Satyagraha

Satyagraha means insistence on truth or firmness in the pursuit of truth. In Gandhi's practice, it involved resisting injustice without violence, accepting personal suffering rather than inflicting it on opponents, and seeking a just resolution through persuasion and moral pressure.

A satyagrahi was expected to remain truthful, avoid hatred and violence, and accept the consequences of peaceful resistance. The objective was not simply to defeat an opponent but to secure correction of an injustice.

Gandhi did not regard satyagraha as passive submission. Participants could actively refuse to obey an unjust order, organise a peaceful strike or withhold a disputed payment. However, they were expected to exercise self-discipline and avoid violence even when subjected to punishment.

How the Principle Was Applied

  • Champaran: Gandhi investigated the grievances of indigo cultivators and refused an official order to leave the district.
  • Ahmedabad: Textile workers maintained a nonviolent strike while seeking a fair wage increase.
  • Kheda: Peasants collectively withheld land revenue while demanding relief following crop failure.

The precise form of resistance therefore depended on the injustice being challenged. Satyagraha was a general method, not a requirement that every movement use the same form of protest.

Chronology of the Early Campaigns

The following sequence establishes the chronological relationship among these events:

  1. January 1915: Gandhi returned to India from South Africa.
  2. December 1916: Rajkumar Shukla approached Gandhi at the Lucknow session of the Indian National Congress and requested his intervention in Champaran.
  3. 1917: Gandhi undertook the Champaran movement in Bihar against the oppressive indigo plantation system.
  4. 1918: Gandhi intervened in the Ahmedabad textile workers' dispute and subsequently led the Kheda revenue satyagraha in Gujarat.
  5. 1919: Gandhi organised the Rowlatt Satyagraha, a much wider campaign against repressive colonial legislation.

Why These Movements Were Important

The earliest Gandhian campaigns connected the national movement with the practical concerns of peasants and workers. They showed that colonial rule and economic exploitation affected different social groups in different ways.

In Champaran, the immediate opponents were European indigo planters supported by an oppressive colonial system. In Ahmedabad, the dispute was between Indian textile mill owners and their workers. In Kheda, peasants challenged the colonial government's demand for land revenue.

The campaigns also demonstrated that resistance and negotiation could operate together. Gandhi organised people to resist injustice while remaining willing to investigate facts, discuss grievances and accept a settlement that provided meaningful relief.

Historical distinction: Gandhi developed satyagraha in South Africa before returning to India. Champaran was his first major satyagraha in India, not the place where he originally invented the method. Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda were localised struggles; they were not nationwide mass movements.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915.
  • Gopal Krishna Gokhale was Gandhi's acknowledged political mentor.
  • Champaran Satyagraha took place in Bihar in 1917.
  • Ahmedabad Mill Workers' Satyagraha took place in Gujarat in 1918.
  • Kheda Satyagraha took place in Gujarat in 1918.
  • The Rowlatt Satyagraha of 1919 was Gandhi's first all-India struggle against British rule.
  • Trap: The Ahmedabad and Kheda movements occurred in the same year but involved different participants and grievances.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12 History, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Theme 13, Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, printed pp. 347-349, 2018-19 edition; NCERT, Class 10 History, India and the Contemporary World II, Nationalism in India, section 1.1, The Idea of Satyagraha; NCERT, Class 8 History, Our Pasts III, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s-1947, printed pp. 115-116, 2020-21 edition.]

title: Gandhi's Early Satyagrahas in India: Background, Principles and Chronology

body:
Background: Indigo Cultivation in Champaran

Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 was Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India. It arose from the exploitation of tenant cultivators by European indigo planters in Champaran district of Bihar.

Indigo was a plant cultivated to produce a blue dye. European planters controlled large plantations and exercised considerable influence over the tenants who cultivated their land. Many tenants were compelled to grow indigo under arrangements that restricted their freedom to choose crops.

The central grievance was the tinkathia system, under which cultivators were required to devote a fixed portion of their holdings to indigo cultivation.

The Tinkathia System

Tinkathia

Tinkathia was a compulsory indigo cultivation arrangement under which tenants in Champaran had to cultivate indigo on 3 out of every 20 parts of their land, equivalent to 15% of the holding.

The name came from the requirement to cultivate indigo on 3 kathas out of 20 kathas. A katha was a local unit of land area.

This system was oppressive because the tenant could not freely decide which crops to cultivate on that portion of the holding. The terms of the arrangement favoured the planters, while the cultivators bore the economic difficulties associated with compulsory production.

Some cultivators also faced unjust payments and penalties connected with indigo arrangements. Consequently, the dispute involved both the freedom to choose crops and relief from oppressive demands.

Tinkathia concerned land under compulsory cultivation. The figure 15% refers to the portion of the holding devoted to indigo. It does not mean that the cultivator was required to surrender only 15% of the harvested indigo.

Rajkumar Shukla and Gandhi's Arrival

Rajkumar Shukla, a peasant from Champaran, played a decisive role in bringing the grievances of the indigo cultivators to Gandhi's attention.

During the Indian National Congress session at Lucknow in December 1916, Shukla approached Gandhi and requested that he personally examine the conditions in Champaran. Shukla continued urging him to visit the district until Gandhi agreed.

In April 1917, Gandhi travelled to Bihar to investigate the situation. His objective was to understand the complaints directly before deciding what action should be taken.

Organisation of the Champaran Movement

Investigation and Local Assistance

Gandhi consulted local people, lawyers and social workers. Important associates included Brajkishore Prasad, Rajendra Prasad and J. B. Kripalani. Local volunteers helped collect information from cultivators and organise the inquiry.

The work involved visiting villages and recording the experiences of tenants. This allowed the movement to present specific grievances rather than relying only on general accusations against the planters.

Refusal to Leave Champaran

British officials considered Gandhi's intervention unwelcome and ordered him to leave the district. Gandhi refused because he believed that abandoning the cultivators would prevent him from fulfilling his responsibility towards them.

He accepted that his refusal could bring legal consequences. On 18 April 1917, he appeared before a court at Motihari, where large numbers of local people had gathered in support.

Gandhi did not attempt to avoid responsibility for disobeying the order. He explained that his duty towards the suffering cultivators required him to remain in Champaran.

The proceedings against him were subsequently withdrawn, and the authorities allowed his inquiry to continue.

The Motihari episode demonstrated a central method of satyagraha: openly refusing an order considered unjust while remaining peaceful and accepting responsibility for the refusal.

Government Inquiry and Negotiated Settlement

As the inquiry continued, evidence of the cultivators' difficulties received wider attention. The Bihar administration eventually appointed an official committee to examine the agrarian grievances.

In June 1917, Lieutenant Governor Sir Edward Gait announced the formation of an inquiry committee that included Gandhi as a member.

The committee examined the complaints and recommended changes in the plantation system. Its principal recommendation was the abolition of compulsory cultivation under tinkathia.

The settlement also involved relief concerning certain unlawful payments extracted from tenants. A compromise provided for the refund of 25% of specified illegally collected payments. The significance of this arrangement was that planters had to concede that their demands could be challenged and reduced.

Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918

The recommendations led to legislative action. The Champaran Agrarian Act was passed on 4 March 1918.

The Act ended the compulsory tinkathia arrangement and helped release cultivators from the obligation to grow indigo under the old coercive system. The cultivators gained greater freedom in deciding what to grow.

Thus, Champaran achieved an important agrarian reform through investigation, organised public support, civil disobedience and negotiation.

Importance and Lessons

The movement established Gandhi as an effective leader of local peasant grievances. It demonstrated that cultivators who had previously feared the planters and local authorities could collectively demand fair treatment.

The campaign also showed that a satyagraha could produce a concrete administrative and legislative outcome without requiring violent confrontation.

Alongside the agrarian campaign, Gandhi and his associates encouraged village education, sanitation and improvement in everyday living conditions. Such activities reflected his view that political action should also address practical social problems.

Champaran's principal achievement was the abolition of compulsory indigo cultivation under tinkathia. The 25% refund concerned particular unlawful collections. It should not be confused with the 15% land requirement under tinkathia or with the crop-yield criterion involved in the Kheda movement.

Prelims focus

  • Year: 1917.
  • Place: Champaran district, Bihar.
  • Main grievance: Compulsory indigo cultivation under the tinkathia system.
  • Tinkathia: Indigo cultivation on 3 out of 20 parts of a holding, or 15%.
  • Important persons: Rajkumar Shukla, Gandhi, Rajendra Prasad and Brajkishore Prasad.
  • Major outcome: Abolition of tinkathia through reforms associated with the Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918.
  • Trap: Rajkumar Shukla invited Gandhi to Champaran; he was not the British official who appointed the inquiry committee.

[Sources: M. K. Gandhi, An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part V, The Stain of Indigo, online text consulted 21 November 2026; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Hundred years of Champaran Satyagraha, 7 April 2017, consulted 21 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12 History, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Theme 13, printed p. 349, 2018-19 edition; Project Management at Champaran: Revisiting Gandhi's Satyagraha, Vikalpa, 2020, DOI 10.1177/0256090920969398, inquiry and recommendations, consulted 21 November 2026.]
